newsitem.title: UK: British widow loses fight to have husband's baby.
newsitem.headline: British widow loses fight to have husband's baby.

text.p: A young British widow was refused permission on Thursday to use her dead husband's sperm to try to conceive his baby through test tube treatment abroad.
Britain's Human Fertilization and Embryology Authority (HFEA) ruled that Diane Blood, 30, could not take the sperm out of Britain.
The Authority had spent a month reconsidering its ban on Blood using the sperm either in Britain or abroad after her case provoked a public outcry. It said it had not changed its mind.

"Solicitors (lawyers) acting for Diane Blood, who is seeking fertility treatment using her deceased husband's sperm, have been told today by the HFEA that it has upheld its decision not to allow the sperm to be exported," it said in a statement.

Blood's case came to public attention in October when she appealed to the High Court to overturn the HFEA's ruling. The judge said he sympathised with her plight but could do nothing to help her because the authority had acted within the law.

The HFEA had ruled that she could not use the frozen sperm because her husband had not left written consent. But after the court case the authority agreed to consider whether the law might allow Blood to take it abroad for treatment.
Doctors in Belgium and the United States said that they were willing to give her in-vitro fertilisation (IVF) treatment.
Blood said waiting for the HFEA's decision had been "just like having a hatchet over your head" but that she planned to take her case to an appeal court.
"Imagine how I would feel for the rest of my life if I had given up on something so important for me," she told reporters.
She said the HFEA had not told her why it had turned down her request once more.
Blood asked doctors to take sperm from her husband while he was on a life support machine after contracting meningitis and going into a coma. It has been kept, frozen, in a British hospital since.
Blood and her husband married in 1991 and she told the High Court that they had been trying for a year before his death to have a baby.

It is the second time this year that the HFEA has been in a controversy. Pro-life groups were outraged in the summer when the authority ordered the destruction of thousands of human embryos created during IVF which had passed their storage date.
